title: Time-Reversal Invariant Topological Photonic Alloy
authors: Feng Ruili, Qu Tiantao, Wu Xianbin, Shi Xiaoxuan, He Mujun, Zhang Lei, Chen Jun
abstract: Conventional approaches generate quantum spin Hall (QSH) and quantum valley Hall (QVH) effects by breaking spatial inversion symmetry across the entire photonic crystal. Consequently, modulating the bulk transmission gaps within these periodic frameworks typically requires global modification of structural parameters throughout the lattice, severely limiting device reconfigurability and post-fabrication adaptability. In this work, we demonstrate that global inversion symmetry breaking is not a prerequisite for inducing topological phases. Instead, local and minimal symmetry breaking is sufficient. Using a photonic alloy platform based on random substitutional disorder in a parallel-plate waveguide, we show that a disorder-driven local breaking of z-direction mirror symmetry and a local breaking of in-plane symmetry are capable of opening topological gaps to trigger QSH and QVH phase transitions, respectively, thereby supporting robust helical edge states and valley kink states. Rigorous topological characterization via the reflection-phase winding method reveals a striking size-dependent scaling behavior in both configurations, where the threshold doping concentration required to trigger the topological phase transition asymptotically vanishes in the thermodynamic limit. By enabling flexible, on-demand bulk gap engineering simply through random doping tuning rather than global structural reconfigurations, this photonic alloy platform not only deepens understanding of disorder induced topological physics but also offers a scalable, highly efficient design strategy for integrated topological optical communications.
summary: The authors show that inducing topological phases (QSH and QVH) in photonic crystals does not require breaking spatial symmetry globally. By introducing controlled, local random substitutional disorder into a photonic alloy, they successfully open topological gaps, enabling flexible, on-demand engineering of edge states using only doping tuning.
main_problem: Conventional methods for inducing topological photonic phases like QSH/QVH require global symmetry breaking, which severely limits device reconfigurability.
main_result: The study demonstrates that local and minimal symmetry breaking via random substitutional disorder is sufficient to open topological gaps and trigger robust helical edge states and valley kink states.
method: Topological characterization is performed using the reflection-phase winding method, analyzing band structures derived from photonic crystal models.
model_or_system: The system is a photonic alloy platform based on random substitutional disorder in a parallel-plate waveguide built on a honeycomb lattice structure.
key_observables: Topological phases (QSH/QVH), Spin Chern Number ($C_s$), reflection phase winding, and bulk transmission gaps.
important_parameters: Doping concentration ($x$), system size (W), and the threshold doping concentration ($x_{th}$) which vanishes in the thermodynamic limit.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that local disorder can effectively mimic global symmetry breaking mechanisms necessary for topological transitions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics of unit cells, band structures showing Dirac points, and phase plots ($\varphi$ vs. $\phi_y$) confirming full winding numbers corresponding to non-trivial topology.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the limitation of global symmetry breaking, then demonstrating QSH via local $z$-mirror symmetry breaking (doping), followed by extending the concept to QVH via in-plane inversion symmetry breaking, consistently using topological invariants for characterization.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful paradigm shift, showing that engineered disorder can induce complex quantum phenomena like topological edge states without requiring perfect global structural control, which is highly relevant for designing robust photonic devices.
